clinicalPearls: A fixed deformity of the intrathoracic trachea in which the coronal (side-to-side) diameter is markedly reduced while the sagittal (front-to-back) diameter is preserved or increased, giving a scabbard-like cross-section.

It is strongly associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is regarded as a radiological marker of long-standing airflow obstruction, typically in older men with a heavy smoking history.
The narrowing is confined to the intrathoracic trachea; the extrathoracic cervical portion is characteristically spared, and the deformity abruptly resolves at the thoracic inlet.
Tracheal cartilage may ossify and the lumen appears flattened laterally on axial CT, with a coronal-to-sagittal ratio well below normal.
Most patients' symptoms reflect the underlying COPD (chronic cough, sputum, dyspnoea) rather than the tracheal shape itself, which is usually an incidental imaging finding.
It should be distinguished from tracheomalacia; in the classic saber-sheath deformity the abnormal shape is relatively fixed, although coexisting expiratory collapse can occur.
The condition is thought to arise from chronically raised intrathoracic pressure and altered mechanical stresses transmitted to the tracheal cartilage over years.
Recognising the pattern prevents misinterpretation as an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative tracheal disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Saber-sheath trachea is a chronic remodelling deformity of the intrathoracic trachea associated with obstructive lung disease. Repeated coughing and the chronically elevated, widely fluctuating intrathoracic pressures generated in COPD are thought to impose abnormal mechanical loading on the tracheal cartilages, leading to lateral flattening with compensatory sagittal widening; the cartilages frequently calcify or ossify and become rigid, so the deformed shape is largely fixed. Because the deforming pressures act within the thorax, the cervical trachea above the thoracic inlet retains its normal rounded contour, producing the characteristic abrupt transition at that level. The altered geometry modestly increases airflow resistance, but the dominant functional impairment in affected patients is the underlying emphysema and small-airways disease rather than the tracheal deformity per se.
additionalDifferentials: tracheomalacia and excessive dynamic airway collapse
extrinsic tracheal compression by goitre or mediastinal mass
additionalInvestigations: chest CT with measurement of coronal and sagittal tracheal diameters
pulmonary function testing to characterise the associated obstructive disease
chest radiograph demonstrating the coronal narrowing on the frontal view
bronchoscopy where an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative process needs exclusion
dynamic expiratory CT if coexisting tracheomalacia is suspected
assessment of smoking history and alpha-1 antitrypsin status where indicated
arterial blood gas or oximetry in advanced obstructive disease
redFlags: new stridor or focal fixed narrowing suggesting a superimposed stenosing lesion
rapidly progressive dyspnoea out of keeping with baseline COPD
features of systemic cartilage disease such as auricular or nasal inflammation
reference.prognosis: The tracheal deformity itself is usually clinically inconsequential and stable, with outcome determined by the severity and management of the underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the coronal narrowing for an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative tracheal disease and pursuing unnecessary intervention.
Overlooking coexisting tracheomalacia by relying only on static inspiratory imaging.
Assuming the deformity accounts for a patient's dyspnoea rather than attributing it to the underlying COPD.
Failing to note that the cervical trachea is spared, a key discriminating feature.
references: Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders, current edition
Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine, current edition
Standard thoracic radiology reference texts on central airway morphology
management: Optimise the underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with inhaled long-acting bronchodilators (long-acting muscarinic antagonists and beta-agonists) and inhaled corticosteroids where indicated
Smoking cessation support as the key modifiable factor driving the airflow obstruction and tracheal remodelling
Pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce exacerbation-related decline
Prompt treatment of infective exacerbations with bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics as appropriate
Reassurance that the fixed tracheal deformity itself needs no specific intervention, reserving airway stenting for the rare case of critical obstruction or coexisting tracheomalacia
Assessment of alpha-1 antitrypsin status where early or atypical obstructive disease is suspected
Serial pulmonary function testing to monitor the severity of the underlying obstructive disease
